purpose: Training/evaluating a citation-checking model. Each item pairs a paragraph + citation against a real, open-access source, labeled for whether the claim accurately reflects what the source actually says.
ground_truth_basis: All sources are real, open-access papers whose abstracts and/or full text were read directly when this dataset was built. The 'source_summary' field paraphrases the relevant findings in the dataset author's own words (no verbatim copying). Verify against the DOI before high-stakes use.

error_types.none: Claim accurately reflects the source and is appropriately attributed.
error_types.misattribution: Claim attributed to a source that does not contain it.
error_types.overstatement: Source makes a weaker, narrower, or more hedged claim than stated.
error_types.distortion: Source's meaning is twisted, oversimplified, or reversed.
error_types.cherry_picking: A real finding is presented in isolation, omitting countervailing findings that change its meaning.
error_types.fabricated_specifics: Real source, but the claim invents specific numbers/details not in it.
error_types.citation_claim_mismatch: Cited source is real but irrelevant to the claim.

severity.subtle: Plausible-looking misrepresentation a careful reader might miss (e.g. dropping a key qualifier, mild overstatement).
severity.moderate: Clear misrepresentation that changes the claim's meaning but stays topically related.
severity.blatant: Egregious error: invented numbers, reversed findings, or wrong source entirely.

sources.citation_apa: Cullen, B., Eichel, K., Lindahl, J. R., Rahrig, H., Kini, N., Flahive, J., & Britton, W. B. (2021). The contributions of focused attention and open monitoring in mindfulness-based cognitive therapy for affective disturbances: A 3-armed randomized dismantling trial. PLOS ONE, 16(1), e0244838.
sources.source_summary: A 3-armed RCT (n=104, adults with mild-to-severe depression and anxiety) compared three 8-week interventions: focused attention (FA), open monitoring (OM), and their combination (MBCT). Key findings: (1) at post-treatment (week 8) all three were broadly comparable across outcomes; (2) they diverged over time and in rapidity and deterioration patterns; (3) FA improved fastest and had the fewest deteriorations for stress and anxiety; (4) OM improved slowest and lost its anxiety gains by week 20, ending with higher anxiety than FA and MBCT (though differences were not statistically significant after correction, p approx .06); (5) MBCT showed the most favorable long-term pattern for depression; (6) the combination (MBCT) did NOT clearly outperform either single component; (7) the authors stress results are preliminary and should be replicated, and note the absence of a non-meditation control group.

sources.citation_apa: Gascon, M. et al.-style greenspace synthesis as represented in: McCormick (2017)/Houlden et al. (2018). The relationship between greenspace and the mental wellbeing of adults: A systematic review. PLOS ONE, 13(9), e0203000.
sources.source_summary: A systematic review of 50 studies on greenspace and adult mental wellbeing. Methodological heterogeneity prevented meta-analysis, so findings were synthesized narratively. Results were mixed: of 8 studies using the GHQ measure of mental distress, all but one found an inverse association between greenspace amount and distress (implying benefit), but regression coefficients varied widely (roughly 0.003 to 0.431). Evidence for quality of life, mental health, and multi-dimensional wellbeing was judged inadequate/mixed. One study found no association for objective greenspace amounts but did find lower distress for higher *perceived* greenness. The review concludes associations exist for some outcomes but evidence is inconsistent overall.

sources.citation_apa: Young, D. K., Carlbring, P., Ng, P. Y., Cheng, D. Y. T., Chen, J. Q., & Ng, S. (2023). Low-intensity online mindfulness-based intervention for university students with anxiety during the COVID-19 pandemic: A randomized controlled trial with 3-month follow-up. Internet Interventions, 33, 100665.
sources.source_summary: An RCT of 134 university students in Hong Kong randomized 1:1 to a low-intensity online mindfulness-based intervention (16 online modules plus two half-day online workshops over 8 weeks) or an inactive control group. Anxiety was measured with the Beck Anxiety Inventory at pre-intervention, post-intervention, and 3-month follow-up. Participants with psychotic disorder, substance use disorder, severe anxiety/depression, or suicide risk were excluded. (Note: this entry's source_summary is based on the published abstract and methods section; the specific effect-size results were not fully read, so items below are restricted to design facts that the abstract states explicitly.)

sources.citation_apa: Lo, J. C., Groeger, J. A., Santhi, N., Arbon, E. L., Lazar, A. S., Hasan, S., von Schantz, M., Archer, S. N., & Dijk, D. J. (2012). Effects of partial and acute total sleep deprivation on performance across cognitive domains, individuals and circadian phase. PLOS ONE, 7(9), e45987.
sources.source_summary: A 2 x 12-day laboratory protocol with 36 participants (18 male; mean age ~27.6) examined how repeated partial sleep deprivation and one bout of acute total sleep deprivation, interacting with circadian phase, affect performance across seven cognitive domains. The sample was stratified by a PER3 polymorphism associated with susceptibility to total sleep deprivation. Performance deteriorated under both partial and total sleep deprivation. A key nuance: sustained attention tasks were highly sensitive to sleep deprivation, but higher-order/executive cognition was comparatively less affected; the data did not straightforwardly support the 'vigilance hypothesis' that sustained attention drives higher cognition, and leaned somewhat toward a 'controlled attention' account in which simpler, more monotonous tasks suffer most. Individuals differed in how affected they were.

sources.citation_apa: Bak, T. H., Nissan, J. J., Allerhand, M. M., & Deary, I. J. (2014). Does bilingualism influence cognitive aging? Annals of Neurology, 75(6), 959-963.
sources.source_summary: An observational study of 853 participants from the Lothian Birth Cohort, first tested in 1947 at age 11 and retested in 2008-2010 in older age. The design's strength is that it controls for childhood intelligence (measured at age 11), addressing the concern that bilinguals and monolinguals might differ at baseline. Finding: bilinguals performed significantly better in later life than predicted from their age-11 baseline cognitive ability, with the strongest effects on general intelligence and reading. The study is observational (it does not establish that learning a second language causes the effect) and concerns later-life cognition, not a claim that bilingualism prevents dementia in this sample.

sources.citation_apa: Brodin, E. et al.-style smartphone cognition study: (2021). Quantifying cognitive impairment after sleep deprivation at different times of day: A proof of concept using ultra-short smartphone-based tests. Frontiers in Psychology / PMC8076531.
sources.source_summary: A proof-of-concept study (N = 182) testing whether 2-minute smartphone-based cognitive tests (the Karolinska WakeApp) could detect effects of sleep deprivation and time of day. After three nights of normal sleep, participants were randomized to either one night of total sleep deprivation or a fourth normal night, then completed brief tests of attention, arithmetic, episodic memory, working memory, and a Stroop conflict task at four timepoints. Finding: sleep deprivation impaired attention, arithmetic, episodic memory, and working memory, but NO effect of sleep deprivation was observed on the Stroop test.

sources.citation_apa: Wang, X. et al. (2023). The strategies of exercise intervention for adolescent depression: A meta-analysis of randomized controlled trials. (PMC9846179).
sources.source_summary: A PRISMA meta-analysis (PROSPERO CRD42022321683) of 13 RCTs comprising 433 adolescents (mean age 10-18) examined exercise interventions for depression. Compared with control, exercise had a moderate antidepressant effect (SMD = -0.65, 95% CI -1.03 to -0.27, p < 0.01). Heterogeneity was substantial (I^2 = 67%). Intervention characteristics (form, frequency, intensity, type, session duration) varied greatly and appeared to moderate the effect. Three studies showed the positive effect persisted up to 40 weeks after the intervention. Because included studies had methodological limitations, the certainty of evidence was rated moderate (GRADE).

sources.citation_apa: Brown, J. C. et al. (2012). The efficacy of exercise in reducing depressive symptoms among cancer survivors: A meta-analysis. PLOS ONE, 7(1), e30955.
sources.source_summary: A meta-analysis of RCTs of exercise interventions in adult cancer survivors, with depressive symptoms as the outcome. It identified 40 exercise interventions including 2,929 cancer survivors (breast cancer survivors in 26 of them). Cancer survivors who completed an exercise intervention reduced depression more than controls, with a small pooled effect (d+ = -0.13, 95% CI -0.26 to -0.01). Increases in weekly volume of aerobic exercise reduced depressive symptoms in a dose-response fashion.

sources.citation_apa: Liu, Y. et al. (2024). Meta-analysis of the effectiveness of exercise as an intervention for suicidal tendency in depressed patients. (PMC12202557).
sources.source_summary: A meta-analysis of 5 RCTs (796 depressed patients) on exercise interventions. Exercise significantly reduced depressive symptoms (SMD = -0.99, 95% CI -1.95 to -0.03, p = 0.04). However, exercise did NOT significantly reduce suicidal ideation severity (SMD = -1.49, 95% CI -4.33 to 1.35, p = 0.30) nor incidents of suicidal ideation (OR = 0.79, 95% CI 0.08 to 7.67, p = 0.84). The confidence intervals on the suicide outcomes were very wide, reflecting few studies and high uncertainty.

sources.citation_apa: Wegner, M. et al. (2025). A 10 years update of effects of exercise on depression disorders in otherwise healthy adults: A systematic review of meta-analyses and neurobiological mechanisms. PLOS ONE, 20(5), e0317610.
sources.source_summary: A systematic review of meta-analyses (an 'umbrella' review) on exercise and depression in otherwise healthy adults, updating Wegner et al. ~10 years earlier. Eleven meta-analytic reviews were included, covering 229 individual studies and 16,255 participants, all based on RCTs. The present review's overall effect size was -0.61. A leave-one-out analysis showed the overall effect was robust (estimates ranged -0.56 to -0.65), indicating no single study drove the result. The review notes that meta-analyses restricted to RCTs tended to report larger effects than those that were not RCT-exclusive.

sources.citation_apa: Allcott, H.-style restriction RCT (2022). Effects of restricting social media usage on wellbeing and performance: A randomized controlled trial among students. PLOS ONE, 17(8), e0272416.
sources.source_summary: A randomized controlled trial among students tracked daily digital activity over three quarters of an academic year. Half were randomly assigned to a treatment restricting social media (Facebook, Instagram, Snapchat) to at most 10 minutes per day. Findings: treatment-group participants substituted other digital activity (instant messaging) for social media and did NOT reduce their total time on digital devices; and, contrary to prior correlational studies, the trial found no significant impact of social media usage (as defined in the study) on wellbeing or performance. The paper situates this against correlational work (e.g., Orben & Przybylski) showing only tiny associations between digital tech use and adolescent wellbeing.

items.paragraph: In a three-armed dismantling trial, focused attention, open monitoring, and their combination (MBCT) produced broadly comparable effects immediately after the 8-week programs, but diverged over the following months in how quickly people improved and in their patterns of deterioration (Cullen et al., 2021).
items.explanation: Accurately reflects the post-treatment parity and the later divergence in rapidity and deterioration that the trial reports.

items.paragraph: A randomized trial demonstrated that combining focused attention and open monitoring in MBCT is clearly superior to either practice alone across all measures of stress, anxiety, and depression (Cullen et al., 2021).
items.explanation: The trial found the opposite on this point: the combination (MBCT) did NOT clearly outperform either single component on any measure or timepoint. The claim reverses a central conclusion.

items.paragraph: Among the three interventions, focused attention showed the fastest improvement and the fewest deteriorations for stress and anxiety (Cullen et al., 2021).
items.explanation: Matches the reported finding that FA had the most rapid improvement and fewest deteriorations on stress and anxiety.

items.paragraph: The study proved that open monitoring meditation is harmful and should never be used for anxiety (Cullen et al., 2021).
items.explanation: The trial found OM improved slowest and lost anxiety gains by week 20, with between-group differences not reaching significance after correction; the authors frame results as preliminary. 'Proved... harmful and should never be used' overstates a hedged, non-significant, preliminary finding.

items.paragraph: The authors caution that, because this is one of the first trials to compare these components and lacked a non-meditation control group, the findings are preliminary and need replication (Cullen et al., 2021).
items.explanation: The paper explicitly states the findings are preliminary, flags the absence of a non-meditation control as a limitation, and calls for replication.

items.paragraph: The trial found that 62% of participants experienced complete remission of their depression after focused attention training (Cullen et al., 2021).
items.explanation: No such '62% complete remission' figure exists in the paper; it reports effect sizes and reliable-change percentages, not a remission rate of this kind. The specific number is invented.

items.paragraph: MBCT showed the most favorable long-term pattern for depression among the three interventions (Cullen et al., 2021).
items.explanation: The paper reports MBCT had the most favorable long-term pattern for depression specifically, even though it did not outperform components overall.

items.paragraph: A systematic review of 50 studies found that the evidence linking greenspace to adult mental wellbeing is mixed, with associations appearing for some measures of mental distress but inadequate or inconsistent evidence for quality of life and broader wellbeing (Houlden et al., 2018).
items.explanation: Accurately conveys the review's central 'mixed evidence' conclusion and the distinction between distress measures and other outcomes.

items.paragraph: A systematic review established that living near greenspace dramatically improves mental wellbeing across all measured outcomes (Houlden et al., 2018).
items.explanation: It selects only the favorable distress findings and presents them as uniform and 'dramatic,' omitting that the review judged evidence for quality of life and multi-dimensional wellbeing inadequate/mixed and that effect sizes varied enormously.

items.paragraph: The review noted that one study found no association with objective greenspace amount but did find lower distress among residents who perceived their neighbourhood as greener (Houlden et al., 2018).
items.explanation: Matches the specific Dzhambov-type finding described in the review: null for objective amount, significant for perceived greenness.

items.paragraph: Because the 50 studies were so methodologically consistent, the authors were able to pool them in a meta-analysis showing a uniform effect size (Houlden et al., 2018).
items.explanation: The opposite is true: methodological heterogeneity *precluded* meta-analysis, so the authors used narrative synthesis, and the coefficients varied widely rather than being uniform.

items.paragraph: A 3-armed randomized trial of meditation found that greenspace reduces anxiety more than focused attention training (Houlden et al., 2018).
items.explanation: The greenspace review is not a meditation trial and makes no comparison to focused attention training; the claim mismatches the cited source entirely (and conflates it with the unrelated mindfulness RCT).

items.paragraph: One randomized controlled trial assigned 134 university students in Hong Kong to either a low-intensity online mindfulness intervention or an inactive control group, measuring anxiety at three points up to a 3-month follow-up (Young et al., 2023).
items.explanation: All design facts (sample size, population, two-arm randomization, online intervention, 3-month follow-up) match the published abstract and methods.

items.paragraph: In a randomized trial of over 5,000 working adults across Europe, an in-person mindfulness retreat eliminated anxiety in the majority of participants (Young et al., 2023).
items.explanation: Nearly every specific is wrong: the study had 134 (not 5,000+) participants, university students in Hong Kong (not working adults across Europe), an online intervention (not an in-person retreat), and the abstract does not claim anxiety was 'eliminated in the majority.'

items.paragraph: The trial excluded individuals with conditions such as psychotic disorder, substance use disorder, severe anxiety or depression, or suicide risk (Young et al., 2023).
items.explanation: Matches the exclusion criteria stated in the methods section.

items.paragraph: In a controlled laboratory protocol, both repeated partial sleep restriction and a single night of total sleep deprivation degraded cognitive performance, though not all domains were equally affected: sustained attention was especially sensitive while higher-order cognition held up comparatively better (Lo et al., 2012).
items.explanation: Captures both the general deterioration and the domain-specific nuance the study emphasizes.

items.paragraph: The study showed that sleep deprivation impairs every cognitive domain equally and to the same degree (Lo et al., 2012).
items.explanation: The central finding is that domains were NOT affected equally; sustained attention was far more sensitive than higher-order cognition.

items.paragraph: Individual differences mattered: the study stratified participants by a PER3 genetic polymorphism linked to differing susceptibility to total sleep deprivation (Lo et al., 2012).
items.explanation: The PER3 stratification and individual variability are explicitly described.

items.paragraph: Across the seven domains tested, sleep deprivation reduced performance by an average of exactly 34% (Lo et al., 2012).
items.explanation: No such single '34%' average impairment figure is reported; the number is invented.

items.paragraph: The authors found that sleep deprivation slightly improved sustained attention while leaving executive function unaffected (Lo et al., 2012).
items.explanation: Reverses the finding: sustained attention was the most impaired (not improved) domain.

items.paragraph: The findings broadly weighed against a strong 'vigilance hypothesis,' since higher aspects of cognition were not much affected even as sustained-attention tasks clearly were (Lo et al., 2012).
items.explanation: Matches the paper's discussion of how its data sit against the vigilance hypothesis.

items.paragraph: In a study following 853 people from age 11 to old age, bilinguals scored better in later life than their childhood cognitive scores would predict, with the strongest effects on general intelligence and reading (Bak et al., 2014).
items.explanation: Accurately reports the longitudinal design, the control for childhood ability, and the domains with strongest effects.

items.paragraph: The study found that bilinguals performed better in later life, attributing this to their higher cognitive ability already present in childhood (Bak et al., 2014).
items.explanation: Inverts the study's logic: its key contribution is that the effect held AFTER controlling for childhood ability, i.e., it was not explained by higher baseline intelligence.

items.paragraph: A longitudinal study proved that learning a second language as an adult prevents dementia (Bak et al., 2014).
items.explanation: The study is observational, examined later-life cognition (not dementia prevention as an outcome here), and cannot establish causation; 'proved... prevents dementia' is far beyond what it claims.

items.paragraph: A notable strength of the study is that it controlled for childhood intelligence measured at age 11, addressing the worry that bilinguals might simply have started out with higher cognitive ability (Bak et al., 2014).
items.explanation: This is precisely the methodological strength the paper highlights.

items.paragraph: A randomized controlled trial assigned 853 children to learn a second language and tracked them for 60 years (Bak et al., 2014).
items.explanation: It was an observational cohort study, not an RCT, and participants were not assigned to learn a language; the design is misrepresented.

items.paragraph: Using ultra-short smartphone-based tests, researchers found that one night of total sleep deprivation impaired attention, arithmetic, episodic memory, and working memory, but did not affect Stroop-task performance (PMC8076531, 2021).
items.explanation: Matches the reported pattern, including the specific null result on the Stroop test.

items.paragraph: The study found that sleep deprivation impaired performance on every test administered, including the Stroop task (PMC8076531, 2021).
items.explanation: Overgeneralizes by sweeping in the Stroop task, which was the one measure showing NO effect of sleep deprivation. Omitting that exception changes the claim.

items.paragraph: A proof-of-concept study randomized 182 participants to a night of total sleep deprivation or a normal night after three nights of normal sleep, then tested cognition at several times the next day (PMC8076531, 2021).
items.explanation: Sample size, randomization structure, and repeated next-day testing all match.

items.paragraph: The smartphone study concluded that sleep deprivation has no measurable effect on cognition (PMC8076531, 2021).
items.explanation: Reverses the main finding: deprivation impaired four of five measured domains; only the Stroop task showed no effect.

items.paragraph: A meta-analysis of 13 randomized controlled trials involving 433 adolescents found a moderate antidepressant effect of exercise compared with control conditions (SMD = -0.65) (Wang et al., 2023).
items.explanation: Effect size, trial count, and sample size all match the meta-analysis.

items.paragraph: The pooled estimate showed substantial heterogeneity across trials, and the authors noted that exercise characteristics such as frequency, intensity, and type varied considerably and may moderate the effect (Wang et al., 2023).
items.explanation: Reflects the reported I-squared of 67% and the discussion of moderators.

items.paragraph: Three of the included studies indicated that the antidepressant benefit of exercise was still present roughly 40 weeks after the intervention ended (Wang et al., 2023).
items.explanation: Matches the reported persistence of effect at 40 weeks in three studies.

items.paragraph: Because the included trials had methodological limitations, the authors rated the overall certainty of the evidence as moderate rather than high (Wang et al., 2023).
items.explanation: Matches the GRADE downgrade to moderate certainty.

items.paragraph: Pooling 40 exercise interventions across 2,929 adult cancer survivors, a meta-analysis found that those completing an exercise program had a small but significant reduction in depressive symptoms relative to controls (Brown et al., 2012).
items.explanation: Intervention count, sample size, and the small significant effect (d+ = -0.13) match.

items.paragraph: The analysis observed a dose-response pattern, with greater weekly volumes of aerobic exercise associated with larger reductions in depressive symptoms (Brown et al., 2012).
items.explanation: Matches the reported dose-response relationship for aerobic volume.

items.paragraph: Most of the included interventions studied breast cancer survivors, with 26 of the 40 interventions focused on that group (Brown et al., 2012).
items.explanation: Matches the composition of the included studies.

items.paragraph: A meta-analysis of 5 randomized controlled trials in 796 depressed patients found that exercise significantly reduced depressive symptoms (Liu et al., 2024).
items.explanation: Trial count, sample, and the significant depression effect (SMD = -0.99, p = 0.04) match.

items.paragraph: Although exercise reduced depressive symptoms in this analysis, it did not significantly reduce suicidal ideation, and the confidence intervals around the suicide-related outcomes were wide (Liu et al., 2024).
items.explanation: Matches the non-significant suicide outcomes and the wide CIs reflecting uncertainty.

items.paragraph: The authors distinguished between exercise's effect on general depressive symptoms and its effect on suicidal ideation, finding support only for the former (Liu et al., 2024).
items.explanation: Accurately separates the significant depression result from the null suicide results.

items.paragraph: An umbrella review of eleven meta-analyses, together covering 229 studies and over 16,000 participants, reported an overall effect size of about -0.61 for exercise on depression in otherwise healthy adults (Wegner et al., 2025).
items.explanation: Counts, participant total, and the -0.61 overall effect size match.

items.paragraph: A leave-one-out analysis suggested the overall effect was robust, since removing any single study left the estimate within a narrow range (Wegner et al., 2025).
items.explanation: Matches the reported leave-one-out range of -0.56 to -0.65.

items.paragraph: The review noted that meta-analyses restricted to randomized controlled trials tended to report larger effects than those that also included non-randomized designs (Wegner et al., 2025).
items.explanation: Matches the discussion contrasting RCT-only versus mixed-design effect sizes.

items.paragraph: In a randomized controlled trial, students assigned to limit social media to ten minutes a day did not reduce their overall time on digital devices, instead shifting toward other activities such as instant messaging (Social media RCT, 2022).
items.explanation: Matches the substitution finding and the absence of a drop in total device time.

items.paragraph: Contrary to earlier correlational research, the trial found no significant effect of restricting social media on students' wellbeing or performance (Social media RCT, 2022).
items.explanation: Matches the null causal finding the trial reports relative to correlational studies.

items.paragraph: The authors situated their null result against large correlational analyses that had found only very small negative associations between digital technology use and adolescent wellbeing (Social media RCT, 2022).
items.explanation: Matches the framing referencing the small associations reported in prior correlational work.

items.paragraph: Each of the three interventions produced medium-to-large improvements on most outcomes, even though they did not differ much from one another at the end of the 8-week programs (Cullen et al., 2021).
items.explanation: Matches the reported effect-size range and post-treatment comparability.

items.paragraph: By the 20-week follow-up, the open monitoring group's anxiety had returned toward pre-treatment levels, ending higher than the focused attention and combined groups (Cullen et al., 2021).
items.explanation: Matches the reported loss of OM anxiety gains by week 20, with the caveat the differences were not significant after correction.

items.paragraph: The laboratory study examined performance across seven cognitive domains, finding that deterioration under sleep deprivation depended on which domain was tested (Lo et al., 2012).
items.explanation: Matches the seven-domain design and the domain-dependent pattern.

items.paragraph: The interaction with circadian phase was central to the design, which crossed sleep deprivation with time of day in a multi-day protocol (Lo et al., 2012).
items.explanation: Matches the protocol's crossing of sleep pressure with circadian phase.

items.paragraph: The sample was drawn from a cohort first assessed in childhood in 1947 and re-assessed in older age decades later, enabling comparison against early-life cognitive scores (Bak et al., 2014).
items.explanation: Matches the longitudinal cohort design and the use of age-11 baseline scores.

items.paragraph: The strongest later-life advantages associated with bilingualism appeared in general intelligence and reading (Bak et al., 2014).
items.explanation: Matches the domains where the study reports the strongest effects.

items.paragraph: Because the 50 included studies differed substantially in methods, the reviewers used narrative synthesis rather than pooling results statistically (Houlden et al., 2018).
items.explanation: Matches the stated reason (methodological heterogeneity) for narrative synthesis.

items.paragraph: Among studies using the GHQ measure, most found that more greenspace was associated with less mental distress, though the strength of the association varied widely across studies (Houlden et al., 2018).
items.explanation: Matches the GHQ pattern and the wide variation in regression coefficients.

items.paragraph: The intervention in this trial consisted of 16 online modules plus two half-day online workshops delivered over eight weeks (Young et al., 2023).
items.explanation: Matches the intervention structure described in the methods.

items.paragraph: Anxiety was assessed with the Beck Anxiety Inventory at three timepoints: before the intervention, immediately after, and at a three-month follow-up (Young et al., 2023).
items.explanation: Matches the stated measure and assessment schedule.

items.paragraph: The cognitive battery in this study was deliberately brief, using two-minute smartphone-based tests to capture attention, arithmetic, memory, and cognitive conflict (PMC8076531, 2021).
items.explanation: Matches the ultra-short smartphone test design and the domains assessed.

items.paragraph: Participants completed a baseline assessment the night before and several further assessments across the following day (PMC8076531, 2021).
items.explanation: Matches the repeated next-day measurement structure.

items.paragraph: Both repeated nights of partial sleep restriction and a single night of total sleep deprivation were associated with worse performance in the study (Lo et al., 2012).
items.explanation: Matches the finding that both partial and total deprivation degraded performance.

items.paragraph: The review followed PRISMA guidelines and pre-registered its protocol before conducting the analysis (Wang et al., 2023).
items.explanation: Matches the PRISMA adherence and PROSPERO pre-registration.

items.paragraph: The meta-analysis focused specifically on randomized controlled trials comparing an exercise intervention with a non-exercise control group (Brown et al., 2012).
items.explanation: Matches the stated inclusion criterion of RCTs with a control group.

items.paragraph: The analysis reported a wide confidence interval for the effect of exercise on suicidal ideation, which crossed the line of no effect (Liu et al., 2024).
items.explanation: Matches the reported CI for suicidal ideation spanning zero (non-significant).

items.paragraph: The 2025 review was framed as a ten-year update to an earlier synthesis, restricting its scope to meta-analyses of randomized controlled trials (Wegner et al., 2025).
items.explanation: Matches the framing as an update and the RCT-only scope.

items.paragraph: Participants' daily digital activity was tracked over roughly three quarters of an academic year in this trial (Social media RCT, 2022).
items.explanation: Matches the tracking period described in the methods.

items.paragraph: Across all timepoints and measures, the combined and open monitoring conditions showed higher average rates of deterioration than focused attention (Cullen et al., 2021).
items.explanation: Matches the reported average deterioration rates (MBCT and OM higher than FA).

items.paragraph: All three mindfulness interventions produced large improvements in anxiety, with clinically significant gains in the majority of participants (Cullen et al., 2021).
items.explanation: The paper reports anxiety was the weakest outcome: only 10-15% showed reliable improvement and 85-90% showed no meaningful change. 'Large gains in the majority' overstates this.

items.paragraph: Focused attention was the slowest of the three interventions to produce improvement (Cullen et al., 2021).
items.explanation: Reversed: focused attention was the fastest to improve, not the slowest; open monitoring was slowest.

items.paragraph: The trial included a waitlist control group that received no meditation, allowing the authors to isolate the specific effect of mindfulness (Cullen et al., 2021).
items.explanation: The study explicitly lacked a non-meditation control group; the authors flag this absence as a limitation. The waitlist control is invented.

items.paragraph: The review found consistent, strong evidence that greenspace improves quality of life across the included studies (Houlden et al., 2018).
items.explanation: Evidence for quality of life was judged inadequate/mixed, not 'consistent and strong'; only some distress measures showed associations.

items.paragraph: Every one of the GHQ studies found that greenspace was associated with reduced mental distress (Houlden et al., 2018).
items.explanation: All but one of the GHQ studies found that association; the claim 'every one' drops the exception.

items.paragraph: The authors concluded that increasing neighbourhood greenspace causes measurable improvements in residents' mental health (Houlden et al., 2018).
items.explanation: A narrative review of mostly cross-sectional studies cannot establish causation; it reports associations of varying strength, not a causal conclusion.

items.paragraph: The trial enrolled university students from several countries to test the online mindfulness program (Young et al., 2023).
items.explanation: Participants came from a single local university in Hong Kong, not several countries.

items.paragraph: Anxiety was measured using a single post-intervention assessment (Young et al., 2023).
items.explanation: Anxiety was measured at three timepoints (pre, post, and 3-month follow-up), not a single post-intervention assessment.

items.paragraph: The study compared the online mindfulness program against an in-person mindfulness program (Young et al., 2023).
items.explanation: The comparator was an inactive control group, not an in-person mindfulness program.

items.paragraph: The study found that executive function was the cognitive domain most severely impaired by sleep deprivation (Lo et al., 2012).
items.explanation: Sustained attention was most sensitive; higher-order/executive cognition was comparatively less affected.

items.paragraph: All 36 participants were affected by sleep deprivation to a near-identical degree (Lo et al., 2012).
items.explanation: The study emphasized individual differences in susceptibility and stratified by a PER3 polymorphism; uniform effect is contradicted.

items.paragraph: The data strongly supported the vigilance hypothesis, confirming that sustained attention governs higher cognition (Lo et al., 2012).
items.explanation: The data did NOT straightforwardly support the vigilance hypothesis; higher cognition was relatively spared even as sustained attention suffered.

items.paragraph: Sleep deprivation was tested only at a single time of day, so circadian effects could not be examined (Lo et al., 2012).
items.explanation: Circadian phase was a central design variable, crossed with sleep deprivation across a multi-day protocol.

items.paragraph: The study showed that bilingualism slows the biological progression of Alzheimer's disease (Bak et al., 2014).
items.explanation: The study examined later-life cognitive test performance in a cohort, not Alzheimer's disease pathology or its biological progression.

items.paragraph: Bilinguals and monolinguals had identical childhood cognitive scores, which is why the later-life difference is attributable to language (Bak et al., 2014).
items.explanation: The study controlled for childhood ability statistically; it does not claim the groups had identical age-11 scores.

items.paragraph: The strongest later-life effects were observed in memory and processing speed (Bak et al., 2014).
items.explanation: The strongest effects were on general intelligence and reading, not memory and processing speed.

items.paragraph: Sleep deprivation impaired performance on the Stroop conflict task along with the other cognitive measures (PMC8076531, 2021).
items.explanation: The Stroop task was the one measure showing NO effect of sleep deprivation; including it misrepresents the result.

items.paragraph: The study used a full hour-long laboratory cognitive battery to detect the effects of sleep loss (PMC8076531, 2021).
items.explanation: The tests were ultra-short two-minute smartphone-based tasks, not an hour-long laboratory battery.

items.paragraph: Participants were sleep-deprived for several consecutive nights before testing (PMC8076531, 2021).
items.explanation: The protocol involved three normal nights followed by one night of total sleep deprivation, not several consecutive deprived nights.

items.paragraph: The meta-analysis reported a large antidepressant effect of exercise in adolescents (Wang et al., 2023).
items.explanation: The reported effect (SMD = -0.65) is characterized as moderate, not large.

items.paragraph: Because heterogeneity was low and the trials were highly consistent, the authors rated the certainty of evidence as high (Wang et al., 2023).
items.explanation: Heterogeneity was substantial (I-squared 67%) and certainty was downgraded to moderate, not high.

items.paragraph: The analysis pooled more than 4,000 adolescents across 13 trials (Wang et al., 2023).
items.explanation: The 13 trials comprised 433 adolescents, not more than 4,000.

items.paragraph: The benefits of exercise disappeared as soon as the intervention ended (Wang et al., 2023).
items.explanation: Three studies showed the positive effect persisted up to 40 weeks after the intervention.

items.paragraph: Exercise produced a large reduction in depressive symptoms among cancer survivors (Brown et al., 2012).
items.explanation: The pooled effect was small (d+ = -0.13), not large.

items.paragraph: The analysis found no relationship between the amount of exercise and the size of the antidepressant effect (Brown et al., 2012).
items.explanation: A dose-response relationship was found: more weekly aerobic volume meant larger reductions in depressive symptoms.

items.paragraph: The meta-analysis was based mainly on prostate cancer survivors (Brown et al., 2012).
items.explanation: Breast cancer survivors dominated (26 of 40 interventions); prostate cancer was examined in only a couple.

items.paragraph: The meta-analysis demonstrated that exercise significantly reduces suicidal ideation in depressed patients (Liu et al., 2024).
items.explanation: Exercise did NOT significantly reduce suicidal ideation (CI crossed zero); only general depressive symptoms improved significantly.

items.paragraph: Drawing on a large evidence base of dozens of trials, the analysis gave precise estimates for suicide-related outcomes (Liu et al., 2024).
items.explanation: Only 5 RCTs were included, and the suicide-outcome confidence intervals were very wide, i.e., imprecise.

items.paragraph: Exercise reduced both depressive symptoms and the incidence of suicidal ideation to a comparable degree (Liu et al., 2024).
items.explanation: Only the depressive-symptom effect was significant; the suicidal-ideation incidence result was non-significant (OR 0.79, CI spanning 1).

items.paragraph: The overall effect of exercise on depression was small, at roughly -0.2 (Wegner et al., 2025).
items.explanation: The reported overall effect size was about -0.61 (moderate-to-large), not -0.2.

items.paragraph: A leave-one-out analysis showed the overall effect was fragile and collapsed when certain studies were removed (Wegner et al., 2025).
items.explanation: The leave-one-out analysis showed the effect was robust (range -0.56 to -0.65), the opposite of fragile.

items.paragraph: The review included non-randomized and observational studies alongside randomized trials (Wegner et al., 2025).
items.explanation: The present review restricted itself to meta-analyses based on RCTs.

items.paragraph: Restricting social media caused a clear improvement in students' wellbeing and academic performance (Social media RCT, 2022).
items.explanation: The trial found no significant effect on wellbeing or performance, contrary to this claim.

items.paragraph: Students told to limit social media sharply reduced their total time spent on digital devices (Social media RCT, 2022).
items.explanation: They substituted other digital activity (instant messaging) and did NOT reduce total device time.

items.paragraph: The study was a large correlational survey of social media users (Social media RCT, 2022).
items.explanation: It was a randomized controlled trial, deliberately distinguished from the correlational studies it contrasts itself with.
